strengths: The paper identifies an important distinction between raw model inputs and human-interpretable explanatory features, and clearly explains why selecting only some macro-level features can introduce latent confounding. This is relevant to researchers working on explainability and model auditing.

Applying FCI with the background knowledge that predictions cannot cause image features is a principled approach under the stated assumptions. PAGs preserve uncertainty about causal relationships, and the discussion usefully acknowledges the limits of observational identification.

The manuscript is generally accessible and makes the proposed workflow concrete through a synthetic example, two annotated-image applications, and preprocessing details. Its synthesis of causal discovery and explainability has an identifiable interested audience.
weaknesses: Necessary—align the empirical conclusions with what the graphs establish. Figure 8 combines definite-cause edges with circle-arrow edges, which remain compatible with pure confounding. Their bootstrap frequency does not establish that a feature is probably causal. Moreover, absence of an adjacent edge does not exclude an indirect causal path. Statements in Section 6.4 and Figures 9–10 identifying likely causes or declaring other features causally irrelevant require separate reporting of edge types and analysis of ancestral paths, or narrower wording.

Necessary—address selection in the X-ray experiment. Section 6.1 selects pneumonia cases and controls with 'no findings,' making inclusion depend on both diagnosis and the explanatory findings. This can introduce selection-induced dependencies, whereas the methodological presentation dismisses selection bias as irrelevant. The manuscript needs to justify an appropriate causal model for this sampling scheme or withdraw the corresponding causal interpretations. Clinical plausibility alone cannot distinguish genuine model determinants from confounded associations.

Necessary—establish the reliability of the conditional-independence tests underlying the real-data results. The bird analysis uses 26 multivalued attributes and nine prediction categories, with conditioning sets up to size four; the X-ray analysis contains only 240 images and potentially rare findings. These settings raise substantial concerns about sparse contingency tables for chi-square tests. Report the actual analysis sample sizes, conditioning-table support, and suitable sensitivity or sparse-data validation. Bootstrap stability does not repair systematically unreliable independence tests.

Necessary—correct or replace the Shapley counterexample. Appendix A.1 evaluates coalitions by substituting feature values while retaining the marginal distribution of the remaining features. For example, its calculation for Z2 does not propagate the stated causal effect Z2→Z1, so it is not the intervention expectation for the supplied SCM. Appendix A.2 retains the unobserved Z3 as a fixed quantity, rather than demonstrating an adjustment calculation available from the observed variables. Define a consistent coalition estimand and recompute the comparison before using it as evidence against the adapted baseline.

Optional improvements—repeated synthetic experiments, controlled interventions on generated shapes, and comparisons using the same annotated features would better characterize practical reliability. The selected LIME/SHAP visualizations primarily demonstrate differences between local pixel attribution and global analysis of annotated features; they provide limited evidence about comparative causal accuracy.
